title: Tahmin edilebilirlik yanılgısı
text: Ask anyone who has lived through a financial crisis and they will describe it as something that was obviously coming. The warnings were everywhere, the reasoning goes; the authorities simply refused to listen. This account is comforting because it implies that the next crisis can be avoided by paying attention. It is also, in most cases, a reconstruction. What actually existed beforehand was a large number of warnings about a large number of possible disasters, most of which never occurred. Once one of them does occur, the human mind performs an operation so automatic that it feels like memory rather than interpretation: it deletes the unrealized warnings and promotes the remaining one to the status of a signal that anybody could have read. Psychologists call the effect hindsight bias, and it has been demonstrated in settings ranging from medical diagnosis to sports commentary. Its practical consequences are considerable. Institutions that believe the last failure was predictable will build systems designed to catch that particular failure, which is rarely the one that arrives next. Worse, the belief makes honest decision-making under uncertainty look like incompetence, since any official who says a risk was genuinely unforeseeable will be assumed to be making an excuse. A more useful discipline, though a much less satisfying one, is to record predictions in writing before the event, with the degree of confidence attached. Organizations that have adopted this practice report an uncomfortable discovery: their experts are neither as accurate nor as consistent as everyone, including the experts, remembered them being.

questions.q: Why is the usual account comforting?
options: It implies the next crisis can be avoided
questions.note: "It implies that the next crisis can be avoided by paying attention."

questions.q: What actually existed before the crisis?
options: Many warnings about many possible disasters
questions.note: Gerçekleşmeyen pek çok uyarı vardı.

questions.q: What does the mind do after the event?
options: It deletes the warnings that did not come true
questions.note: "It deletes the unrealized warnings and promotes the remaining one."

questions.q: What institutional mistake follows from the bias?
options: Building systems for the last failure
questions.note: Geçen sefer olan başarısızlığı yakalamaya ayarlı sistemler kuruluyor.

questions.q: What discipline does the author recommend?
options: Recording predictions with confidence levels beforehand
questions.note: Olaydan önce yazılı ve güven derecesi belirtilmiş tahmin.

questions.q: What did organizations discover?
options: Their experts were less accurate than remembered
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Kurumun hafızası
text: When a long-serving employee retires, the organization loses two things. The first is obvious: a set of skills, which can be replaced through recruitment. The second is harder to name and almost impossible to advertise for. It consists of knowledge about why particular arrangements exist. Every institution accumulates rules that appear arbitrary to newcomers, and a proportion of them genuinely are. Others are the residue of an expensive mistake that nobody now remembers making. The person who can distinguish between the two is usually someone who was present when the mistake occurred. Once that person leaves, the organization faces an unattractive choice: preserve every rule out of caution, and gradually become unable to move, or clear away the ones that look pointless and periodically rediscover why they existed. Consultants tend to recommend the second, partly because the first produces no visible achievement. The most careful organizations attempt a third approach. Before removing a rule, they require somebody to write down what the rule appears to prevent, and to circulate that note widely enough that anyone who remembers the original reason has an opportunity to object. The method is slow and is frequently ignored under pressure, but where it has been maintained it converts institutional memory from something stored in individuals into something stored in a process, which retirement cannot take away. The difficulty is that the benefit appears only in the form of mistakes that were never repeated, and nobody is promoted for those. A practice whose value is invisible tends to survive only where somebody senior keeps insisting on it, which is itself a kind of institutional memory and equally fragile.

questions.q: What is the first loss when an employee retires?
questions.note: "The first is obvious: a set of skills."

questions.q: What does the second kind of knowledge consist of?
questions.note: "Knowledge about why particular arrangements exist."

questions.q: What are some apparently arbitrary rules?
options: The residue of a forgotten mistake
questions.note: "The residue of an expensive mistake that nobody now remembers making."

questions.q: What is the risk of preserving every rule?
options: The organization becomes unable to move
questions.note: "Gradually become unable to move."

questions.q: What does the third approach require?
options: Keeping all rules for ten years
Writing down what a rule appears to prevent
questions.note: Kural kaldırılmadan önce neyi önlediği yazılıp duyuruluyor.

questions.q: What is the benefit of the third approach?
options: Memory is stored in a process, not in individuals
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Çevirinin görünmezliği
text: A translation is generally praised when it does not feel like one. Reviewers commend a novel for reading fluently in its new language, which sounds like an obvious compliment until you consider what it requires. To produce that fluency the translator must remove everything that would remind the reader of the original: unfamiliar rhythms, sentence structures that resist the target language, references that would demand a footnote. The result is a text that the reader can absorb without effort, and which quietly conceals the labor that produced it. A number of translators have argued that this convention does the original a disservice. A novel written in a language with a different relationship to time or formality is not simply the same story in other words; the strangeness is part of what is being communicated. Translations that preserve some of that strangeness are harder to read and are routinely criticized as clumsy, even when the clumsiness is faithful. The dispute is not merely aesthetic. Publishers rarely name translators on covers, and contracts frequently deny them royalties, arrangements that follow logically from the belief that a translator transfers a text rather than writes one. Where campaigns have succeeded in putting translators' names on covers, sales have not fallen, which suggests the invisibility was never a commercial necessity so much as an inherited habit that nobody had been asked to defend. The habit is now weakening for a practical reason as well as a moral one. Readers who follow a translator across several authors have begun to treat that name as a guide to quality, in the way they once followed an editor or a publishing house. A profession that spent a century being praised for disappearing may turn out to have a readership of its own.

questions.q: When is a translation usually praised?
options: When it does not feel like a translation
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: What must the translator remove to achieve fluency?
options: Anything reminding the reader of the original
questions.note: Yabancı ritimler, dirençli yapılar, dipnot gerektiren göndermeler.

questions.q: What do some translators argue?
options: The strangeness is part of the message
questions.note: "The strangeness is part of what is being communicated."

questions.q: How are faithful but strange translations received?
questions.note: "Routinely criticized as clumsy, even when the clumsiness is faithful."

questions.q: What follows from seeing translation as transfer?
options: No name on the cover and no royalties
questions.note: Bu inançtan mantıken bu düzenlemeler çıkıyor.

questions.q: What happened when translators were named?
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Gürültünün maliyeti
text: Noise is the pollutant that legislation reaches last, partly because it leaves no residue. Smoke can be photographed and contaminated water can be sampled, but a sound that damaged somebody's sleep two hours ago has vanished entirely. This has consequences for how the harm is treated. Where air quality is monitored continuously and published, noise is typically measured after a complaint, at a time chosen by the authority, and expressed as an average that smooths away exactly the events that cause the damage. A road that is silent for six hours and unbearable for twenty minutes can produce a respectable average. Medical research has steadily strengthened the case for taking the problem seriously. Long-term exposure to traffic noise is associated with elevated blood pressure and with disturbances to sleep architecture that persist even when the sleeper reports no awareness of being woken. The mechanism appears to be that the auditory system does not switch off; it continues to assess sounds for threat throughout the night. Remedies exist and are mostly unglamorous: quieter road surfaces, lower speed limits, restrictions on night deliveries, and building regulations that treat sound insulation as seriously as heat insulation. What is missing is not technology but a way of registering the harm, since a population that sleeps badly rarely knows what it is losing and therefore rarely demands anything. A few cities have begun to publish continuous noise measurements in the same form as air quality data, street by street and hour by hour. The effect has been immediate and slightly awkward for the authorities, because residents who can point at a chart stop being treated as complainers and start being treated as witnesses.

questions.q: Why does legislation reach noise last?
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: What is the problem with averages?
options: They smooth away the damaging events
questions.note: Yirmi dakikalık dayanılmaz gürültü ortalamada kayboluyor.

questions.q: What does long-term exposure affect?
questions.note: "Elevated blood pressure and ... disturbances to sleep architecture."

questions.q: Why does sleep suffer even without awareness?
options: The auditory system keeps assessing threat
The body needs silence to breathe
questions.note: İşitme sistemi gece boyunca kapanmıyor.

questions.q: What does the author say is missing?
options: A way of registering the harm
questions.note: "What is missing is not technology but a way of registering the harm."

questions.q: Why do affected populations rarely demand action?
options: They do not know what they are losing
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Amatörün geri dönüşü
text: For most of the twentieth century, expertise moved in one direction. A discipline professionalised, established qualifications, and the amateurs who had founded it were politely shown to the door. Astronomy is the standard example: the wealthy enthusiast with a private telescope gave way to institutions with instruments no individual could afford. What has happened over the past two decades is therefore unexpected. Amateur astronomers now contribute a substantial proportion of observations of variable stars and are frequently the first to report a supernova, because professional telescopes are scheduled months in advance and cannot simply look at whatever happens to be interesting tonight. Similar patterns appear elsewhere. Volunteers with modest equipment record birdsong across whole countries, producing datasets that no funded project could match for coverage. The relationship is not without friction. Professionals complain, sometimes justifiably, about data collected without consistent method, and amateurs complain that their contributions are absorbed into papers where they appear, if at all, in an acknowledgement. The collaborations that function best have an explicit division of labor: the amateurs supply breadth and persistence, the professionals supply instruments and analysis, and both are named. What makes the arrangement possible is not goodwill but a particular kind of problem — one where the limiting factor is attention distributed over time and space, which is precisely the resource that institutions find hardest to buy. It is worth noticing that this reverses the usual anxiety about volunteers. The fear was always that unpaid contributors would undercut professional work; what has happened instead is that they have occupied the part of the field professionals were structurally unable to reach.

questions.q: What happened to amateurs during the twentieth century?
options: They were pushed out as disciplines professionalised
questions.note: "The amateurs who had founded it were politely shown to the door."

questions.q: Why can amateurs report supernovae first?
options: Professional telescopes are scheduled in advance
questions.note: Profesyonel teleskoplar aylar öncesinden programlanıyor.

questions.q: What do volunteer birdsong projects achieve?
options: Coverage no funded project could match
questions.note: "Producing datasets that no funded project could match for coverage."

questions.q: What do amateurs complain about?
questions.note: Katkıları makalelerde ancak teşekkür bölümünde görünüyor.

questions.q: What do the best collaborations have?
questions.note: "An explicit division of labor."

questions.q: What makes such arrangements possible?
options: The limiting factor is attention over time and space
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Ölçmenin bozduğu şey
text: A hospital that is judged on waiting times will reduce waiting times. This sounds like a success, and sometimes it is. But the target does not specify how the reduction should be achieved, and administrators under pressure will find the cheapest route. Patients may be recorded as having been seen when a nurse takes their name; difficult cases may be moved to a different list; appointments may be offered at hours nobody can attend, so that a refusal counts as a patient choice rather than a delay. None of this requires dishonesty on the part of any individual. It requires only that a number matters more than the thing the number was invented to describe. Economists have written about this pattern for decades, and it appears wherever performance is managed from a distance: in schools judged on pass rates, in police forces judged on recorded crime, in charities judged on the proportion of donations spent on programs. The lesson usually drawn is that targets are harmful, but that conclusion is too convenient, because the alternative — trusting institutions without evidence — has its own long record of failure. A more demanding response is to treat every measure as temporary, to change it before anyone has learned to satisfy it artificially, and to pay attention to the people who deliver the service, who generally know exactly which numbers have become theater and which still mean something. That last group is systematically the least consulted, because consulting them requires admitting that the measure was always an approximation. An administrator who asks a nurse which figures are honest is opening a conversation that cannot be closed again, and the reluctance to open it is not stupidity but self-preservation.

questions.q: What happens when a hospital is judged on waiting times?
options: It reduces them, by whatever route is cheapest
questions.note: İlk üç cümle.

questions.q: What does the text say about individual dishonesty?
questions.note: "None of this requires dishonesty on the part of any individual."

questions.q: Where else does the pattern appear?
questions.note: Uzaktan yönetilen her yerde.

questions.q: Why is 'targets are harmful' too convenient?
options: Trusting institutions without evidence also fails
questions.note: Alternatifin de uzun bir başarısızlık sicili var.

questions.q: What does the author recommend instead?
questions.note: "To treat every measure as temporary."

questions.q: Who knows which numbers have become theater?
options: The people who deliver the service
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Sessiz bırakma
text: The phrase arrived suddenly and was immediately misunderstood. Quiet quitting does not describe leaving a job; it describes doing the job as written and declining to do more. The debate that followed revealed less about young workers than about the assumptions of everybody else. Managers who described the behavior as laziness were, without quite saying so, admitting that their teams had been staffed on the understanding that people would work beyond their contracts. Defenders of the practice were equally quick to overstate their case, presenting the refusal of unpaid effort as a form of resistance rather than as a plain contractual position. What both sides tended to avoid was the question of what extra effort had actually been buying. In organizations where discretionary work led reliably to promotion, few people withdrew it. Where it had become a permanent expectation attached to no reward, the withdrawal was not a generational mood but a rational adjustment, and it had been occurring quietly for years before anybody produced a name for it. The most useful consequence of the phrase, whatever its accuracy, is that a large number of managers were obliged to look at their own job descriptions and notice how much of the work was being done by goodwill that appeared nowhere in writing. A few organizations went further and wrote the extra duties down, which had the useful effect of making them negotiable. Once a task appears in a document it can be costed, assigned or removed, whereas an expectation that lives only in habit can be neither refused nor rewarded, and tends to fall on whoever is least able to object.

questions.q: What does quiet quitting actually describe?
options: Doing the job as written and no more
questions.note: İkinci cümle.

questions.q: What were critical managers implicitly admitting?
options: Teams were staffed assuming extra unpaid work
questions.note: Sözleşmenin ötesinde çalışılacağı varsayımıyla kadro kurulmuş.

questions.q: How did defenders overstate the case?
options: They presented it as resistance rather than a contractual position
questions.note: "Presenting the refusal of unpaid effort as a form of resistance."

questions.q: Where did few people withdraw extra effort?
options: Where it reliably led to promotion
questions.note: "Where discretionary work led reliably to promotion, few people withdrew it."

questions.q: How does the author describe the withdrawal?
options: A rational adjustment, not a generational mood
questions.note: "Not a generational mood but a rational adjustment."

questions.q: What was the useful consequence of the phrase?
options: Managers examined how much work depended on goodwill
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Şehrin altındaki nehir
text: Under most old cities there is at least one river that no longer appears on any map. As settlements grew, small watercourses became convenient drains, then health hazards, and were finally covered over and forgotten. For a century this was regarded as progress. The reversal of that judgment began not with environmental campaigns but with flooding. A buried river still carries water, and when heavy rain exceeds the capacity of the pipe it was forced into, the water returns to its original route, which is now occupied by basements and car parks. Engineers discovered that restoring a stretch of river to the surface was frequently cheaper than enlarging the pipe, and that the restored section absorbed storm water in a way no drain could match. The projects that followed produced effects nobody had costed. Property values along the reopened sections rose, which was welcome to owners and less welcome to tenants. Streets that had been shortcuts became destinations, and traffic patterns changed across whole districts. Ecologists recorded species returning within two seasons. None of this means that every covered river should be opened; some run beneath structures that cannot be moved, and reopening others would displace communities who have no say in the matter. It does suggest that a decision taken for one reason, by a generation that could not imagine an alternative, is not automatically the right decision now. Several cities have therefore begun to map their buried watercourses before any proposal is made, on the reasonable ground that a public argument about a river is only possible once people know the river is there. The maps have proved popular in a way the engineers did not anticipate, and in two cases residents have asked for a stream to remain covered, which is also a decision worth having made deliberately.

questions.q: Why were small rivers covered over?
options: They became drains and then health hazards
questions.note: İkinci cümle.

questions.q: What began the reversal of that judgment?
questions.note: "Began not with environmental campaigns but with flooding."

questions.q: What did engineers discover?
options: Reopening was often cheaper than enlarging the pipe
questions.note: "Frequently cheaper than enlarging the pipe."

questions.q: Which effect was welcome to owners but not to tenants?
questions.note: "Welcome to owners and less welcome to tenants."

questions.q: Why should not every river be reopened?
options: Some run under structures that cannot be moved
questions.note: "Some run beneath structures that cannot be moved."

questions.q: What is the author's general point?
options: An old decision is not automatically right now
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Uzman tanığın sorunu
titleEn: The Problem of the Expert Witness
text: Courts need specialist knowledge and have no reliable method of evaluating it. A judge who must decide whether a building collapsed because of a design fault cannot personally assess structural engineering, and so the system relies on expert witnesses. The arrangement contains an obvious tension: the expert is chosen and paid by one side. Most experts are honest, and the dishonest ones are rarely caught lying outright. The distortion operates more subtly, through selection. A lawyer who consults five specialists and instructs the one whose preliminary view is most favorable has not corrupted anybody; they have simply filtered. The court then hears two confident opinions and has no way of knowing that eight other specialists were never called. Several jurisdictions have experimented with remedies. Court-appointed experts remove the selection problem but introduce another, since the single appointed voice acquires enormous influence and cannot be tested by disagreement. Requiring both experts to meet before the hearing and produce a joint statement of what they agree on has proved more useful, because it narrows the dispute to the genuine point of difference and exposes areas where a confident claim was not shared by anybody else in the field. The reform is unglamorous, costs almost nothing, and is resisted mainly by those whose advantage lay in the confusion. Judges who have used the procedure describe a further benefit that is harder to quantify. When the two experts have already agreed on eighty per cent of the technical ground, the remaining disagreement becomes legible to a non-specialist, and the court can concentrate on the question it is actually competent to decide: not which account of the physics is correct, but which witness has given reasons rather than assertions.

questions.q: What tension does the arrangement contain?
options: The expert is chosen and paid by one side
questions.note: "The expert is chosen and paid by one side."

questions.q: How does the distortion usually operate?
questions.note: "The distortion operates more subtly, through selection."

questions.q: What does the court not know?
options: That other specialists were never called
questions.note: "No way of knowing that eight other specialists were never called."

questions.q: What problem do court-appointed experts create?
options: A single voice that cannot be tested by disagreement
questions.note: Tek atanmış görüş büyük etki kazanıyor ve sınanamıyor.

questions.q: What has proved more useful?
options: A joint statement of what the experts agree on
questions.note: Duruşmadan önce ortak beyan hazırlamak.

questions.q: Who resists the reform?
options: Those whose advantage lay in the confusion
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Yeniden okumanın değeri
text: Reading lists are built on the assumption that quantity is the measure. Students record how many books they have finished, applications ask what you have read, and the culture rewards breadth. Rereading, by contrast, looks like inefficiency: why return to a book you already know when so many remain unopened? The objection assumes that a book is a container of information which, once transferred, need not be visited again. That description fits a manual and almost nothing else. With any text whose meaning depends on structure, the first reading is spent discovering what happens; only on a second reading can attention be given to how the thing is made, because the reader is no longer occupied with suspense. Writers describe this experience unanimously and readers rarely believe them until they try it. There is also a less comfortable argument. A book you reread at thirty and again at fifty produces different results, not because the text changed but because you did, which makes rereading one of the few available instruments for measuring your own movement. The practice has a cost, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest: an hour spent rereading is an hour not spent discovering something new, and a reader who only returns to familiar books gradually stops being challenged at all. What seems defensible is a ratio rather than a rule, and a willingness to notice which of the two activities you are currently avoiding. Libraries, which have no commercial reason to prefer one over the other, have quietly encouraged the practice for years by keeping the same editions on the shelf for decades. A reader who returns to the same building and the same copy is being offered a measurement instrument, whether or not anybody describes it that way.

questions.q: What assumption do reading lists rest on?
questions.note: İlk cümle.

questions.q: What description of a book does the objection assume?
questions.note: "A container of information which, once transferred, need not be visited again."

questions.q: What becomes possible on a second reading?
options: Attention to how the text is made
questions.note: Okur artık merakla meşgul olmadığı için yapıya bakabiliyor.

questions.q: Why does rereading at different ages give different results?
questions.note: "Not because the text changed but because you did."

questions.q: What cost does the author admit?
options: An hour rereading is an hour not spent discovering
questions.note: "An hour spent rereading is an hour not spent discovering something new."

questions.q: What does the author finally recommend?
options: A ratio rather than a rule
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Uzmanlığın devredilemeyen kısmı
text: Every organization that loses an experienced person discovers the same thing at roughly the same speed. The tasks were documented. The procedures were written. What has gone is the layer underneath, which nobody thought to record because nobody had ever articulated it. An engineer of thirty years knows which of the readings on a panel is the one that actually matters, and knows it in a way that survives no attempt at explanation, because the knowledge is not a rule but a very large number of remembered exceptions. Asked to write it down, such a person produces a document that is accurate, complete and useless, since the useful part was never a sentence. The standard response to this problem is documentation, which addresses the part that was never the problem. The responses that work are slower and more awkward. Pairing, in which the successor watches ordinary work for months rather than being taught. Deliberate overlap, in which a departure is planned a year in advance and the two people share responsibility without either being formally in charge. Both are expensive, and both are the first things canceled when a budget tightens, which is how organizations reliably arrange to lose the thing they least intended to. What makes the loss hard to see is that nothing fails immediately. The new person follows the written procedure and gets a correct result for eleven months. The failure arrives on the first occasion that falls outside the procedure, and by then the person who would have recognized it has been gone long enough that nobody connects the two events.

questions.q: What is lost when an experienced person leaves?
options: The layer nobody thought to record
questions.note: "What has gone is the layer underneath."

questions.q: Why is the engineer's knowledge hard to write?
options: It is remembered exceptions, not a rule
questions.note: "The knowledge is not a rule but a very large number of remembered exceptions."

questions.q: What is wrong with the standard response?
options: It addresses a part that was never the problem
questions.note: "Documentation, which addresses the part that was never the problem."

questions.q: What happens to pairing and overlap in a tight budget?
options: They are given to outside firms
questions.note: "Both are the first things canceled when a budget tightens."

questions.q: Why is the loss hard to see?
questions.note: "What makes the loss hard to see is that nothing fails immediately."

title: Bir sayının kariyeri
text: A number enters public life through a recognizable sequence. It begins as an estimate in a study, surrounded by the conditions under which it holds. A press office removes the conditions, because a headline cannot carry them. A newspaper removes the word estimate. A second newspaper, reporting the first, removes the source. Within a month the figure is a fact, repeated by people who would be astonished to learn that it was ever a range. The mechanism deserves more attention than the individual errors it produces, because it operates identically on numbers that happen to be true. Nothing in the process selects for accuracy; it selects for portability, and the qualities that make a figure travel are shortness, roundness and the absence of any accompanying condition. A carefully bounded estimate of between eleven and nineteen per cent will lose every race to a confident fifteen. What can be done about this is limited and worth doing anyway. Journalists who print the range rather than the midpoint are read slightly less and are right considerably more often. Researchers who refuse to supply a single figure are treated as difficult and are usually protecting something real. The most useful habit available to an ordinary reader is to ask, on encountering any striking number, what it was before somebody made it memorable. The question is answerable more often than it looks. A figure that has survived the journey intact will usually still carry the word about, or a range, or the name of the body that produced it, and a figure that has lost all three has almost certainly been through the process described here. This is not a test of truth, since a number can be stripped of its conditions and remain correct. It is a test of how much weight the figure can bear, which is a different question and the one that actually matters when somebody is using it to argue for something.

questions.q: What does a press office remove?
questions.note: "A press office removes the conditions."

questions.q: What does the process select for?
questions.note: "Nothing in the process selects for accuracy; it selects for portability."

questions.q: Which figure travels better?
options: A range of eleven to nineteen
questions.note: "Will lose every race to a confident fifteen."

questions.q: What does the writer say about journalists who print ranges?
questions.note: "Are read slightly less and are right considerably more often."

questions.q: What habit does the writer recommend?
options: Ask what the number was before it was made memorable
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Mimarlıkta korumacılık
titleEn: Keeping the Front and Losing the Building
text: A practice has grown up in cities under pressure to build, in which the front wall of a historic building is retained and everything behind it is demolished and replaced. The result satisfies the letter of the protection and empties it of meaning. Defenders of the approach argue, not unreasonably, that the alternative is either a museum city that cannot house anybody or the loss of the front as well. Both consequences are real, and the argument would be stronger if the practice were confined to buildings whose interiors had genuinely been lost. In a considerable number of cases the interior was structurally sound and simply inconvenient. What the practice reveals is a confusion about what protection was ever for. A building is not valuable because of the arrangement of stone visible from the pavement; it is valuable because of the relationship between that arrangement and the rooms it implies, and a façade with a different building behind it is a sentence with the verb removed. Critics sometimes overstate their case by implying that nothing may change, which is indefensible in a city that needs housing. The stronger position accepts substantial change and asks a narrower question: whether what remains still explains itself. A converted warehouse whose windows are in the wrong places for its new use passes that test. A stone front with eleven floors of glass behind it does not, and no amount of architectural language makes the difference invisible to somebody standing on the street.

questions.q: What does the practice do?
options: Keeps the front and replaces everything behind
questions.note: "The front wall... is retained and everything behind it is demolished."

questions.q: When would the defenders' argument be stronger?
options: If it were used only where interiors were truly lost
questions.note: "If the practice were confined to buildings whose interiors had genuinely been lost."

questions.q: What does the writer say a building's value depends on?
options: The relationship between the front and the rooms it implies
questions.note: "The relationship between that arrangement and the rooms it implies."

questions.q: How do critics sometimes overstate their case?
questions.note: "By implying that nothing may change, which is indefensible."

questions.q: What is the narrower question the writer prefers?
options: Whether what remains still explains itself
questions.note: "Whether what remains still explains itself."

title: Gönüllü yardımın zararı
text: After a disaster, donations of clothing arrive in quantities that nobody requested and almost nobody can use. The consequences are well established among people who do this work and almost unknown outside it. Sorting the material consumes the labor of staff who are needed elsewhere. Storing it occupies space that is required for supplies that were requested. Disposing of what cannot be used costs money that was donated for something else, and in several documented cases the cost of destroying unwanted clothing has exceeded its value when new. The same pattern appears with volunteers who arrive without being asked, who must be housed and fed and supervised by an operation already at its limit. None of this is a reason to doubt the generosity. It is a reason to notice that generosity, expressed in the wrong form, transfers the cost of the donor's feelings onto the people being helped. The organizations that handle this well have stopped explaining the economics, which persuades nobody, and have started making the alternative equally satisfying: a photograph of the specific thing a given amount actually bought, sent to the person who sent the money. It works because the problem was never that people are stupid about aid. The problem is that writing a number into a form feels like nothing, and filling a box with coats feels like helping. That asymmetry is not a failure of intelligence and it will not be argued away. It is the same reason that people who will not give blood will queue for hours to carry water, and any organization that treats it as ignorance rather than as a fact about human beings will keep receiving lorries of clothing it cannot use, along with letters expressing surprise that the gratitude was not warmer.

questions.q: What does sorting donated clothing consume?
options: The labor of staff needed elsewhere
questions.note: "Sorting the material consumes the labor of staff who are needed elsewhere."

questions.q: What has exceeded the clothing's new value?
questions.note: "The cost of destroying unwanted clothing has exceeded its value when new."

questions.q: What is the problem with unasked volunteers?
options: They must be housed, fed and supervised
questions.note: "Who must be housed and fed and supervised."

questions.q: What does misdirected generosity transfer?
options: The cost of the donor's feelings onto those helped
questions.note: "Transfers the cost of the donor's feelings onto the people being helped."

questions.q: What works better than explaining the economics?
options: A photograph of what the money actually bought
questions.note: "A photograph of the specific thing a given amount actually bought."

title: Sınav sisteminin kendi kendini bozması
titleEn: The Target That Ate the Purpose
text: Any measure used to judge performance eventually stops measuring what it was chosen to measure, and the mechanism is not corruption but attention. A hospital judged on waiting times will reduce waiting times, and the reduction will be genuine; what is invisible in the figure is which activities were quietly moved aside to achieve it. A school judged on the proportion of students reaching a threshold will concentrate its effort on the students closest to that threshold, because that is where the effort produces the most movement in the number. Neither institution has cheated. Both have responded rationally to the question they were asked, and the trouble is that the question was a summary of the purpose rather than the purpose itself. The proposed remedies are mostly worse than the disease. Adding more measures multiplies the distortions and consumes the time of the people being measured. Removing measures altogether returns power to whoever is most confident. What survives contact with practice is narrower: keep the measure, publish it, and require the institution to report alongside it a small number of things that the measure would predictably damage. A school that reports its threshold figure next to the performance of its weakest quarter has not solved the problem, but it has made the trade-off visible to the people who chose it, which is the most that any system of measurement can honestly promise. The objection to this is that it makes the institution look worse, and that objection is correct. A school publishing both figures will be compared unfavorably with one publishing only the flattering one, at least until the practice becomes general. This is the ordinary difficulty of going first, and it is the reason such changes almost never come from the institutions themselves. They come from whoever is in a position to require the second figure from everybody at once.

questions.q: What is the mechanism behind the problem?
questions.note: "The mechanism is not corruption but attention."

questions.q: What does a school judged on a threshold do?
options: Concentrates on students closest to it
questions.note: "Will concentrate its effort on the students closest to that threshold."

questions.q: What is wrong with adding more measures?
options: It multiplies distortions and consumes time
questions.note: "Adding more measures multiplies the distortions."

questions.q: What happens if measures are removed?
options: Power returns to whoever is most confident
questions.note: "Removing measures altogether returns power to whoever is most confident."

questions.q: What does the writer recommend?
options: Report the measure next to what it would damage
questions.note: "Require the institution to report alongside it a small number of things that the measure would predictably damage."

title: Tarafsızlık iddiası
text: A reporter who gives equal space to two positions has done something that looks like fairness and may be its opposite. Where the evidence genuinely divides a field, balance describes the situation accurately. Where it does not, the same practice manufactures a disagreement that exists only on the page, and does so in a form the reader cannot detect, since nothing in the article discloses the proportions outside it. The defense usually offered is that the reader should decide. This sounds respectful and quietly transfers to the reader a task the reader cannot perform, because the information needed to weigh the two accounts is precisely what has been left out. A reader who is told that some researchers hold one view and others hold another has been given no way of knowing whether the split is nine to one or one to nine, and in most disputes that ratio is the entire question. The alternative is not to suppress the smaller position, which would be both dishonest and unwise, since fields have been wrong before and the correction usually starts small. It is to report the position and the weight it carries in the same sentence. Journalists resist this because it requires a judgment, and judgments can be criticized in a way that quotation cannot. That is true, and it is also the job. A newspaper that will not weigh evidence has not avoided taking a position; it has taken the position that all positions are equally supported, which is a claim about the world and one that is very often false.

questions.q: When is balance accurate?
options: Where the evidence genuinely divides a field
questions.note: "Where the evidence genuinely divides a field, balance describes the situation accurately."

questions.q: Why can the reader not detect the problem?
options: Nothing in the article discloses the proportions
questions.note: "Nothing in the article discloses the proportions outside it."

questions.q: What is wrong with 'the reader should decide'?
options: The reader lacks the information needed to decide
questions.note: "The information needed to weigh the two accounts is precisely what has been left out."

questions.q: Why should the smaller position not be suppressed?
questions.note: "Fields have been wrong before and the correction usually starts small."

questions.q: What position does a newspaper take by refusing to weigh evidence?
options: That all positions are equally supported
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Kariyer değiştirmenin gerçek maliyeti
titleEn: Counting the Cost of Starting Again
text: People considering a change of career calculate the salary they will forgo and stop there, which understates the cost in one direction and overstates it in another. The understatement is the loss of position within a hierarchy of competence. A person with fifteen years in a field does not merely earn more; they are consulted, their judgment is trusted without explanation, and a great deal of their working day runs on a credit that was accumulated slowly and cannot be transferred. Moving means being the person whose suggestions are politely noted. Very few people who describe the financial arithmetic mention this, and a considerable number of those who return to their old field name it as the reason. The overstatement lies in the assumption that the fifteen years are lost. In practice the portable part is larger than it looks, and it is rarely the technical part. Knowing how a decision actually gets made, how to tell a real deadline from a performance, and how to say no without damage: these survive the move intact, and their value in a new field is frequently higher, because the people who have them are scarcer there. The honest summary is that the transferable skills are real and the transferable status is not. A person who understands this before moving tends to plan for eighteen difficult months and to be pleasantly surprised. A person who does not tends to interpret the eighteen months as evidence of a mistake.

questions.q: What do people usually calculate?
options: The salary they will give up
questions.note: "People... calculate the salary they will forgo and stop there."

questions.q: What is the hidden loss?
options: Position within a hierarchy of competence
questions.note: "The loss of position within a hierarchy of competence."

questions.q: What does the writer say is portable?
options: Knowing how decisions actually get made
questions.note: "Knowing how a decision actually gets made... these survive the move intact."

questions.q: Why is that knowledge more valuable in a new field?
options: The people who have it are scarcer there
questions.note: "Because the people who have them are scarcer there."

questions.q: How does an unprepared person read the first eighteen months?
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Kentin gece hayatı kimin
text: The argument about noise in a city center is usually presented as residents against businesses, which is accurate about the parties and misleading about the substance. What is actually in dispute is the order in which people arrived and what that entitles them to. A person who buys a flat above a bar that has operated for thirty years has a weaker case than one whose quiet street acquired a bar last spring, and most legal systems recognize some version of this, though rarely in a form that resolves anything. The practical difficulty is that both changes happen at once. Districts become desirable because they are lively, which raises prices, which brings residents who can afford the prices and did not come for the liveliness. Within a decade the venues that created the value are closed by complaints from people who moved there because of them. Several cities have tried to break this loop by attaching the obligation to the building rather than the occupant. A flat built near an existing venue must be constructed to a higher standard of insulation, and the cost falls on the developer who profits from the location rather than on the business that was there first. Where this has been tried it has worked better than any system of curfews, and it has one property that makes it politically survivable: it does not require anybody to decide who was right. The objection raised by developers is that the requirement makes some sites unbuildable, and in a small number of cases that is true and is the intended effect. A flat that cannot be built to a standard where its occupant will sleep is a flat that will generate complaints for as long as it stands, and permitting it transfers a permanent problem to the venue in exchange for a single sale.

questions.q: What is actually in dispute?
options: Who arrived first and what that entitles them to
questions.note: "What is actually in dispute is the order in which people arrived."

questions.q: What is the loop the writer describes?
options: Liveliness raises prices, which brings people who close the venues
questions.note: "The venues that created the value are closed by complaints from people who moved there because of them."

questions.q: What have several cities attached to the building?
questions.note: "Attaching the obligation to the building rather than the occupant."

questions.q: Who pays under that system?
options: The developer who profits from the location
questions.note: "The cost falls on the developer who profits from the location."

questions.q: Why is the approach politically survivable?
options: Nobody has to be declared right
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Kötü haberi erken vermek
titleEn: The Cost of Waiting to Tell
text: Organizations that discover a problem almost always delay the announcement, and the reasons given are almost always reasonable in isolation. The facts are incomplete. A partial statement would cause unnecessary alarm. The investigation should be allowed to establish what happened before anybody speaks. Each of these is true, and their combined effect is a delay that converts a manageable failure into a scandal about concealment, which is a considerably worse thing to be accused of than the original error. The pattern is consistent enough to be treated as a law. What the delay actually purchases is not accuracy but the appearance of control, and it purchases it from the wrong account. Every week of silence increases the probability that the information will emerge through somebody else, and the difference between an organization that discloses and an organization that is caught is the difference between a bad month and a decade of distrust. Institutions that handle this well share one uncomfortable habit. They have decided in advance, in writing, what threshold of evidence triggers disclosure, and they have decided it at a moment when no incident is in progress. The rule is not written to be wise; it is written to be binding on people who will, at the relevant moment, be frightened, defensive and entirely convinced that this particular case is different. That conviction is worth taking seriously as a symptom rather than an argument. It arrives in every case, including the ones that later turn out to have been ordinary, and an organization that has felt it four times and been wrong four times has learned something that no amount of reasoning in the moment will supply. The rule exists to carry that learning across into a week when nobody can remember it.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the reasons for delay?
questions.note: "The reasons given are almost always reasonable in isolation."

questions.q: What does the delay convert the failure into?
questions.note: "Converts a manageable failure into a scandal about concealment."

questions.q: What does the delay actually purchase?
questions.note: "What the delay actually purchases is not accuracy but the appearance of control."

questions.q: What is the difference between disclosing and being caught?
options: A bad month against a decade of distrust
questions.note: "The difference between a bad month and a decade of distrust."

questions.q: Why is the rule written in advance?
options: To bind people who will later be frightened and defensive
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Klasiklerin yeniden çevrilmesi
titleEn: Why Translations Age Faster Than Books
text: A novel written two centuries ago can still be read without difficulty in its own language, while a translation made sixty years ago often feels distinctly older than the original. The reason is not that translators write badly. It is that a translation is a reading, and a reading is made of the assumptions of its moment: what counts as natural speech, what may be said directly, which foreign words a reader is expected to know. The original carries its age openly, and the reader adjusts. The translation carries two ages at once, and the second is invisible, which is why it grates. This has a consequence that publishers understand and readers often resent. Retranslation is not a commercial trick but a structural necessity, and a literature that stops retranslating gradually loses access to works it believes it possesses. The resentment is understandable. A reader who loved a particular version is being told that the book they loved was partly the translator's, which is true and unwelcome. The most useful thing a new edition can do is decline to pretend otherwise. Editions that print a short note explaining what the previous translator was trying to achieve, and where the new one has decided differently, convert an apparent insult into the only thing it actually is: evidence that somebody has been reading the book closely for two hundred years. There is a limit to how far this can be pushed. A work retranslated every fifteen years by publishers competing for the same small market produces versions that differ mainly in their marketing, and readers are right to be suspicious of a new edition whose only visible argument is that it is new. The distinction is not difficult to draw in practice, and it rests on whether the translator can say what the previous version got wrong.

questions.q: Why does a translation age faster?
options: It is made of the assumptions of its moment
questions.note: "A translation is a reading, and a reading is made of the assumptions of its moment."

questions.q: What does the writer say about the original's age?
options: It is carried openly and the reader adjusts
questions.note: "The original carries its age openly, and the reader adjusts."

questions.q: What is retranslation described as?
questions.note: "Retranslation is not a commercial trick but a structural necessity."

questions.q: Why do readers resent it?
options: The book they loved was partly the translator's
questions.note: "The book they loved was partly the translator's, which is true and unwelcome."

questions.q: What should a new edition do?
options: Explain what the previous translator was trying to achieve
questions.note: "Editions that print a short note explaining what the previous translator was trying to achieve."

title: Bağışlanan koleksiyon
text: A private collector who leaves a collection to a public institution almost always attaches conditions, and the conditions are almost always the part that causes trouble thirty years later. The most common is that the works must be displayed together and in the arrangement the donor chose. This sounds modest and is not. A museum that accepts it has agreed to give a permanent room to a particular taste, and taste is the one thing in a collection guaranteed to date. Rooms of this kind exist in most large institutions, and they are recognizable at once: well lit, carefully maintained, and visited chiefly by people looking for the way out. The institutions are not free to reconsider, since the condition was the price of the gift and the family is usually still watching. Refusing such gifts is harder than it looks. A curator who declines a significant collection on the grounds that the conditions are unwise will be overruled by a board that sees a valuable acquisition at no cost, and the curator will have left by the time the difficulty becomes visible. The compromise that works is dull and requires patience: accept the collection, agree to display it in full for a fixed term of perhaps twenty years, and record in the same document what happens afterwards. Donors resist this, which is informative. A gift intended to enrich a collection survives a time limit without difficulty. A gift intended to secure a reputation does not.

questions.q: What is the most common condition?
options: The works must never be sold
The room must be free to enter
The works must stay together in the donor's arrangement
questions.note: "The works must be displayed together and in the arrangement the donor chose."

questions.q: Why is that condition not modest?
options: It gives a permanent room to a taste that will date
questions.note: "Taste is the one thing in a collection guaranteed to date."

questions.q: Why is refusing such gifts hard?
options: A board sees a valuable acquisition at no cost
questions.note: "Will be overruled by a board that sees a valuable acquisition at no cost."

questions.q: What compromise does the writer suggest?
options: Display in full for a fixed term, then reconsider
questions.note: "Agree to display it in full for a fixed term of perhaps twenty years."

questions.q: What does resistance to a time limit reveal?
options: The gift was meant to secure a reputation
questions.note: Son iki cümle.

title: Kurallara harfiyen uymak
text: When workers in a dispute decide to follow every written procedure precisely, the operation slows to a degree that surprises everybody including the workers. This is generally reported as a tactic, and it is, but the interesting part is what it demonstrates about ordinary weeks. A system that fails when its rules are obeyed exactly was never running on its rules. It was running on continuous small judgments about which rule to relax, and those judgments were being made by people who were never asked to make them, are not paid for making them, and would be disciplined if a relaxation went wrong. Management responses divide predictably. The common one is to treat the slowdown as bad faith, which is accurate as a description of the intent and useless as an analysis of the mechanism. The rarer one is to ask which rules were being quietly ignored and why, and this occasionally produces the discovery that a procedure written eleven years ago for equipment that no longer exists has been formally in force and universally disregarded throughout. Neither response resolves the dispute, which is about something else. But an organization that has been through this and taken the second route emerges with a rulebook that describes what it actually does, which is rarer than it should be and worth more than the argument that produced it. There is a reason this outcome is uncommon. Rewriting a rulebook to match practice requires somebody senior to put in writing that a rule has been broken for years with the knowledge of everybody involved, and the natural instinct is to restate the rule instead and hope. That instinct is understandable and it guarantees a repeat performance, because the pressures that produced the informal relaxations are still there on the Monday after the dispute ends.

questions.q: What does the slowdown demonstrate?
options: The system was never running on its rules
questions.note: "A system that fails when its rules are obeyed exactly was never running on its rules."

questions.q: Who was making the small judgments?
options: People never asked or paid to make them
questions.note: "Made by people who were never asked to make them, are not paid for making them."

questions.q: What is the common management response?
options: Treat the slowdown as bad faith
questions.note: "The common one is to treat the slowdown as bad faith."

questions.q: What can the rarer response discover?
options: Rules in force for equipment that no longer exists
questions.note: "A procedure written eleven years ago for equipment that no longer exists."

questions.q: What does an organization taking the second route gain?
options: A rulebook describing what it actually does
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Deniz seviyesinden önce gelen
text: Coastal planning concentrates on the level of the sea, which is measurable and rises slowly, and pays much less attention to the thing that reaches a town decades earlier. Salt moves through ground water long before any street is under water, and it moves horizontally through soil in a way that is invisible from the surface until wells turn brackish and trees that have stood for a century begin to die from the roots. A community can therefore lose its agriculture, its drinking water and a substantial share of its property value while every photograph of the coastline looks reassuringly unchanged. Defences designed against waves do nothing about this, since the water is not arriving over anything. What makes the problem politically difficult is that it has no moment. A storm produces a date, a photograph and a budget. A gradual rise in the salt content of a well produces a series of slightly worse harvests and an argument about whether the farmer is managing the land properly. By the time the pattern is undeniable the affordable responses have usually expired. The places that have handled it best are the ones that began monitoring wells thirty years before they expected trouble, which is an unglamorous program to fund and the only one that produces the evidence at the moment it can still be used. The cost of such monitoring is trivial next to any of the responses it later makes possible, which is the usual shape of this kind of problem and the usual reason it is not done. A budget line that pays for readings nobody is alarmed by is indistinguishable, in a difficult year, from a budget line that pays for nothing at all.

questions.q: What arrives decades before the sea?
questions.note: "Salt moves through ground water long before any street is under water."

questions.q: How is the change first noticed?
options: Wells turn brackish and old trees die
questions.note: "Wells turn brackish and trees... begin to die from the roots."

questions.q: Why do wave defences not help?
options: The water is not arriving over anything
questions.note: "Since the water is not arriving over anything."

questions.q: Why is the problem politically difficult?
questions.note: "What makes the problem politically difficult is that it has no moment."

questions.q: What have the best-prepared places done?
options: Monitored wells thirty years in advance
questions.note: Son cümle.

title: Mülakatın ölçtüğü şey
text: The unstructured interview, in which a manager talks to a candidate for forty minutes and forms an impression, is among the most thoroughly studied selection methods and among the least predictive. Its accuracy is close to that of a brief work sample and considerably below that of a structured conversation in which every candidate is asked the same questions in the same order and scored against agreed criteria. These findings have been stable for decades and have changed practice remarkably little, which is itself the interesting fact. The explanation is not ignorance. Managers who know the evidence continue to trust their impressions, and the reason they give, when pressed, is that the structured version feels mechanical and prevents them from following up something interesting. This is accurate, and it is precisely the mechanism by which the unstructured version fails: following up something interesting means spending the available time on whatever the candidate happened to make vivid, and vividness is not evidence. There is a further difficulty that rarely appears in the research. An interview is not only a measurement; it is the candidate's first experience of the organization, and a process that treats them as a set of scores communicates something true about what the job will be like. The firms that have resolved this tend to run the structured assessment and then add a separate, explicitly unscored conversation whose purpose is to let the candidate decide. That second conversation is worth protecting from the first. As soon as anything said in it can affect the outcome, the candidate returns to performing and the organization loses the only part of the process in which it might have heard something true about how it looks from outside.

questions.q: How accurate is the unstructured interview?
options: Close to a brief work sample and below structured methods
questions.note: "Its accuracy is close to that of a brief work sample and considerably below that of a structured conversation."

questions.q: What is the interesting fact?
options: The findings have changed practice very little
questions.note: "Have changed practice remarkably little, which is itself the interesting fact."

questions.q: What reason do managers give?
options: Structure prevents following up something interesting
questions.note: "The structured version feels mechanical and prevents them from following up something interesting."

questions.q: Why is that reason the mechanism of failure?
options: Time goes to whatever is vivid, and vividness is not evidence
questions.note: "Vividness is not evidence."

questions.q: What further difficulty does the writer raise?
options: The interview is the candidate's first experience of the organization
questions.note: "An interview is not only a measurement; it is the candidate's first experience."

title: Uzun vadeli tahminlerin ömrü
text: Long-range forecasts are produced in enormous quantities and are almost never scored, which is the single most important fact about them. A prediction made for ten years hence is consumed in the month it is published, and by the time it could be evaluated the publication has moved on, the author has revised the view without announcement, and the audience has forgotten the original wording. The absence of scoring is not an accident of publishing schedules. It is what allows the activity to continue in its present form, since a forecaster whose record was tracked would be obliged to express uncertainty, and expressed uncertainty is commercially worthless. The small research literature that has tracked forecasts finds the expected result: confident specific predictions perform worse than hedged vague ones, and the forecasters most in demand are drawn disproportionately from the confident group. What is less expected is that the better forecasters are not distinguished by expertise in the subject. They are distinguished by the habit of revising in small increments as evidence arrives, and by a marked reluctance to defend a position they have already stated. This is an unappealing set of professional qualities. It produces people who are frequently right, rarely quoted, and almost never invited back a second time. The practical consequence for a reader is straightforward and slightly depressing. The forecaster worth attending to is identifiable in advance, but not by the qualities that make a forecast enjoyable to read. The test is whether the person has publicly changed their mind about something specific, and said so without being forced to, which almost nobody in the business has ever done.

questions.q: What is the most important fact about long-range forecasts?
questions.note: "Are almost never scored, which is the single most important fact about them."

questions.q: Why is the absence of scoring not an accident?
options: It allows the activity to continue in its present form
questions.note: "It is what allows the activity to continue in its present form."

questions.q: What does the research find?
questions.note: "Confident specific predictions perform worse than hedged vague ones."

questions.q: What distinguishes the better forecasters?
options: Revising in small increments as evidence arrives
questions.note: "The habit of revising in small increments as evidence arrives."

questions.q: What is the result of those qualities?
questions.note: Son cümle.
